tile-installation.title: Tile Installation Sarasota FL | Porcelain & Wood-Look
tile-installation.description: Porcelain, wood-look and large-format tile installed to TCNA spec on Sarasota and Manatee County slabs. 2026 pricing from $6 per sq ft, free estimate.
tile-installation.h1: Tile Installers for Sarasota and Manatee County Homes
tile-installation.lede: Tile is unforgiving of shortcuts underneath it, and on a Florida slab the substrate work decides whether a floor lasts twenty years or has to come back out in three.
tile-installation.capsule: Tile installation in Sarasota and Manatee County covers porcelain, ceramic, wood-look plank and natural stone, set with TCNA-spec substrate prep and movement joints built in from the start. 2026 installed pricing runs $6 to $22 per square foot depending on format and material, with large-format porcelain and natural stone at the top of that range. Most single rooms set and grout within a week.
tile-installation.near_me_html: Tile installers near me searches usually come from two very different places: barrier-island condos on Longboat Key needing an HOA-compliant floor, and inland slab homes in Palmetto, Bradenton, Sarasota, Venice, Nokomis and North Port replacing thirty-year-old ceramic. We work both ends of that range, from a single condo bathroom to a full first-floor re-tile. Tile crews typically need an extra vehicle trip for setting materials and grout on barrier-island jobs, which we build into the schedule rather than into the estimate. If you're calling from Longboat Key specifically, that page covers elevator scheduling and building approval in more depth.

sections.h2: Why large-format and wood-look tile need flatter substrates
sections.html:
Large-format porcelain and long wood-look planks are less forgiving of an uneven substrate than small-format tile ever was. ANSI A108.02 sets the bar for any tile with an edge 15 inches or longer: the substrate can vary no more than 1/8 inch over 10 feet and 1/16 inch over 24 inches. A slab that meets code for 12-inch tile can still be too wavy for a 30x60 porcelain panel, which is why we measure flatness with a laser level before quoting large-format work, not after the tile arrives. A 1,600-square-foot open living and kitchen area in a 1990s Sarasota ranch, for example, needs at least two interior movement joints running through the layout under EJ171 spacing, plus a tighter perimeter joint anywhere the tile ties into a sliding-door threshold that sees direct sun.

Wood-look porcelain plank runs long and narrow, often 6x36 or 8x48, and that aspect ratio makes lippage the visible failure mode rather than cracking. We set wood-look plank with leveling clips on every joint and keep grout lines tight, close to the width a real hardwood seam would show, so the finished floor reads as wood from across the room instead of tile pretending to be wood.

Where a floor already has old tile down, the substrate underneath is often the bigger unknown than the tile on top. Our tile removal service handles the demo and thinset chip-out with dust-controlled equipment, and where the substrate underneath still isn't flat enough, our slab leveling crew levels it before new tile goes down.

sections.h2: Movement joints, TCNA spec and why tile cracks
sections.html:
Tile itself doesn't crack from foot traffic; it cracks when the slab underneath moves and the tile has nowhere to absorb that movement. TCNA's EJ171 standard calls for movement joints every 20 to 25 feet in each direction on interior tile, tightening to every 8 to 12 feet anywhere the tile sees direct sunlight or moisture, including lanais and sunrooms. In a small bathroom or bedroom, a perimeter gap hidden under the baseboard is usually enough; open-concept living areas need visible joints worked into the layout.

We plan movement joints into the layout before we set the first tile, not after, because a joint added later never looks intentional and a joint skipped never gets a second chance once the grout is in. On slab additions or rooms with a lot of west-facing glass, we tighten our own spacing below the 20-foot TCNA maximum.

Condo buildings often layer their own rules on top of TCNA spec: sound-transmission requirements, work-hour windows, freight-elevator booking. Our condo flooring page and the condo approval checklist tool cover what HOAs typically ask for before tile goes down in a multi-story building.

sections.h2: Why tile goes hollow or pops loose
sections.html:
A hollow sound under tile almost always means it's lost its bond to the substrate, and that's rarely one single cause. Industry failure analysis describes tenting and hollow tile as compounding defects: missing movement joints combined with poor mortar bond or a contaminated substrate. Skip the movement joints, skimp on mortar coverage, or set tile over dust and sealer residue, and you get some combination of both.

Once tile has debonded, patching over the hollow spot doesn't fix it; the tile has to come back out, the substrate corrected, and the tile reset with full mortar coverage. Our floor repair team handles that pull-and-reset work, and our blog post on diagnosing hollow tile covers how to tell a cosmetic issue from a structural one before you call anyone. Hollow tile calls cluster in older housing stock more than new construction, since decades of foot traffic and slab settling give a marginal original installation more time to fail; a 1980s or 1990s Sarasota or Bradenton home with its original ceramic is a common source of these calls. Fixing one hollow section without checking the rest of the room is a common shortcut that leaves a homeowner back on the phone within a year, which is why the tap survey covers the whole floor every time, not just the spot someone pointed to.

PEI is the wear-rating scale tile carries, running 0 to 5: PEI 2 suits light traffic like a bathroom, PEI 3 covers every residential floor, and PEI 4 to 5 is built for heavy residential and commercial use. Porcelain, by ANSI definition, absorbs 0.5% or less water by weight, which is what lets it carry PTCA certification and hold up in a wet bathroom or lanai transition the way a higher-absorption ceramic body can't. Grout choice affects long-term maintenance as much as tile choice does. Epoxy grout resists staining and doesn't need sealing, which makes it our default for kitchen and high-traffic floors; sanded cement grout costs less upfront but needs periodic sealing to keep it from absorbing stains, particularly in a lanai-adjacent kitchen that tracks in outdoor dirt.

Tile for a floor that gets walked on wet needs a wet DCOF, dynamic coefficient of friction, of 0.42 or higher under ANSI A137.1 and A326.3, and that number is a floor, not a guarantee, for every condition. Pool decks, lanais and shower pans typically call for more traction than the interior minimum provides. We steer clients toward textured or matte porcelain in showers, primary bathrooms and lanai transitions rather than the glossy finishes that look sharp in a showroom and turn slick the first time they get wet.

Natural stone floors need a different slip-resistance conversation than porcelain, since sealing and finish, honed versus polished, affect traction as much as the stone itself. We recommend a honed or flamed finish over polished stone in showers and lanai-adjacent rooms, and we reseal natural stone at each maintenance visit rather than treating sealer as a one-time step.

A typical bathroom floor sets in a day, with grout going in the next day; manufacturer guidance allows foot traffic 24 hours after grouting and 72 hours before heavy loads or appliances go back down. Larger rooms with a movement-joint layout, a waterproofing system, or a herringbone pattern add time for planning and cutting, not just square footage. A whole-house tile job of 1,800 to 2,500 square feet typically runs one and a half to two weeks including tear-out. Condo work-hour restrictions can stretch that timeline further; many associations limit construction noise to weekday business hours, which turns a two-day tile job into four calendar days even though the actual labor hasn't changed. For a full price breakdown by size and format, see our tile installation cost guide.

faqs.q: What DCOF rating keeps a tile floor from being slippery when wet?
faqs.a: ANSI A137.1 and A326.3 set 0.42 as the minimum wet DCOF for a level interior floor that gets walked on wet. That's a floor, not a guarantee, for every condition: pool decks, lanais and shower pans typically need more traction than the interior minimum provides, which is why we steer those areas toward textured or matte finishes instead of high-gloss tile.

faqs.q: What's the actual difference between porcelain and ceramic tile?
faqs.a: Porcelain, by ANSI A137.1 definition, absorbs 0.5% or less water by weight when tested under ASTM C373; that low absorption is what lets it carry PTCA certification and hold up in wet Florida bathrooms, lanais and exterior-adjacent spaces. Ceramic bodies generally absorb more, which is fine indoors but makes porcelain the safer default anywhere near water.

faqs.q: Does tile need movement joints in every room?
faqs.a: Every tile installation needs somewhere to move, but not every room needs a visible joint. Small rooms can hide a perimeter gap under the baseboard; larger open areas and anything that sees direct sun or moisture need visible movement joints spaced per TCNA's EJ171 standard, roughly every 20 to 25 feet indoors and tighter outdoors or in sunlit rooms.

faqs.q: Can new tile go directly over an existing hollow-sounding tile floor?
faqs.a: No. Hollow tile has already lost its bond, and setting new tile over a failed substrate just carries the problem forward. That area needs to come out, the substrate corrected, and new tile set with full mortar coverage, the same pull-and-reset process our floor repair crew uses on any debonded tile.

faqs.q: Wood-look tile vs LVP: which makes more sense here?
faqs.a: Wood-look tile wins in flood-exposed ground floors, lanais and homes that sit closed up all summer, because porcelain ignores water and heat. LVP wins on comfort, speed and price, at $2.75 to $5.50 per square foot installed against $8 to $13 for wood-look porcelain plank in 2026. The longer comparison is in LVP or porcelain tile for a Florida house.
